intro:
These exercises build toward one operational truth: a broker decouples services in time, but it does not decouple you from the consistency, idempotency, and observability work that asynchronous handoff requires. You start by pinning down who owns each routing decision, then trace and extend the exact-match exchange, and finally encode the commit-then-ack ordering that keeps acknowledged work from being lost.

The later exercises move from mechanics to policy. You distinguish a transient failure that deserves a bounded retry from a poison message that belongs in a dead-letter queue, you make the handler idempotent so at-least-once delivery becomes harmless, and you design a versioned envelope so a message can outlive the code that produced it. Throughout, the rule is the same one the chapter states plainly: an ack is a promise the work is safely done, and a queue is a place work can pile up invisibly unless you watch it.

exerciseSolutions.title: Separate routing-key choice from routing policy
exerciseSolutions.solution:
When a producer publishes, it controls exactly one thing: the routing key, a stable semantic label such as orders.created that describes what happened, not where it should go. The producer never names a queue. The exchange controls everything else. It owns the binding state, the table that maps routing keys to the set of queues that should receive a copy, and it owns the routing policy, the rule that decides for a given key which bindings match. The producer says what happened; the exchange decides who hears about it.

This split is what lets a new team add a search-indexing queue for orders.created without touching any publisher. They declare a queue and bind it to the routing key orders.created on the existing exchange. The next message published with that key now copies into their queue as well, because routing topology lives in exactly one place, the exchange, and the publisher was never queue-aware to begin with. Nothing about the producer's code, deployment, or contract changes. If routing topology lived in the producer instead, every new consumer would force an edit to and a redeploy of every publisher, which is precisely the coupling the broker exists to remove.

A message whose routing key matches no binding produces zero deliveries. It is not an error and it is not delivered anywhere; the exchange simply finds no matching queues. The chapter's model counts this as an unrouted message rather than silently discarding it because a key with no binding usually means a misconfiguration, a typo in the key, a queue that was never declared, or a binding that was removed by mistake, and a silent drop hides that. A visible unrouted counter turns a routing gap into a metric you can alarm on instead of a message that vanished without a trace.
criteria: States the producer chooses only the routing key while the exchange owns binding state and routing policy.
Explains a new queue bound to an existing key receives copies with no change to any publisher.
States an unbound key yields zero deliveries and is tracked as unrouted rather than delivered or silently dropped.

exerciseSolutions.title: Trace the idempotent consumer's state transitions
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The Consumer in Example 2 runs every delivery through one ordered decision machine in on_delivery. First it checks processed_ids: if the message_id is already present, it counts a duplicate and returns without redoing the work. Otherwise it inspects the order_id. If the order is ord-fail and attempt is below 3, it counts a retry and pushes a clone with attempt incremented onto retry_queue; if ord-fail has reached attempt 3, it pushes the delivery to the dlq. Any other order is treated as success: processed is incremented and the message_id is recorded in processed_ids. Only the success path mutates processed_ids, so only success makes a future copy a duplicate.

msg-1 arrives twice. The first delivery has order_id ord-1, which is not ord-fail, so it takes the success branch: processed becomes 1 and msg-1 is inserted into processed_ids. The second msg-1 now finds its id already in processed_ids, so it takes the duplicate branch: duplicates becomes 1 and it returns without touching the work. This is the idempotency guard absorbing a redelivery exactly as designed.

msg-2 carries order_id ord-fail at attempt 1. Its id is not yet seen, so it falls through to the ord-fail branch; attempt 1 is below 3, so retried becomes 1 and a clone with attempt 2 is queued. The drain loop pops that clone: attempt 2 is still below 3, so retried becomes 2 and a clone with attempt 3 is queued. The drain loop pops that clone: attempt 3 is not below 3, so it takes the dlq branch and dlq now holds 1 entry. Note that ord-fail is never recorded in processed_ids on any path, which is correct, because it never succeeded. Finally msg-3 with order_id ord-3 succeeds, making processed 2. The printed output is therefore processed = 2, duplicates = 1, retried = 2, dlq = 1.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Step-by-step trace of on_delivery showing each branch and the final counter values.
criteria: Identifies the second msg-1 as a counted duplicate that returns without redoing work.
Shows ord-fail retried at attempts 1 and 2, then moved to the DLQ when attempt reaches 3.
Predicts processed = 2, duplicates = 1, retried = 2, dlq = 1.

exerciseSolutions.title: Add a wildcard topic match to the exchange
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Keep the exact-match path exactly as it is and add wildcard support as a second, separate store. Exact bindings stay in the HashMap keyed by the full routing key, so an exact lookup remains a single O(1) hash probe. Wildcard bindings go in their own collection of (pattern, queue) pairs, because a pattern such as orders.* cannot be looked up by hash; it must be matched segment by segment against the incoming key. Splitting the two stores means the common case, an exact key with no wildcards, pays no scanning cost, and only the wildcard set is iterated.

Matching splits both the binding pattern and the routing key on '.' and compares segment by segment. A '*' segment matches exactly one segment, never zero and never several, so orders.* matches orders.created and orders.cancelled but not orders or orders.created.eu. The pattern matches only when the two segment counts are equal and every segment is either identical or a '*'. This is the single-trailing-wildcard rule the exercise asks for; it deliberately does not implement the multi-segment '#' wildcard, which would match a variable number of segments.

The new route_topic method returns the union of the exact-match queues and the wildcard-match queues with no duplicates. A routing key can legitimately match both an exact binding and a wildcard binding, for example orders.created bound directly to billing and also covered by orders.* bound to audit, and each target queue must appear once. The implementation guards against duplicates by checking membership before pushing (or equivalently by collecting into a set and back into a Vec). A key that matches neither store returns an empty Vec<String>, preserving the chapter's unrouted-versus-routed distinction.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Exact bindings stay in the hash map; a separate wildcard set is matched segment by segment and unioned without duplicates.
criteria: Binding orders.* makes its queue resolve for both orders.created and orders.cancelled via route_topic.
The unchanged route method still resolves exact bindings such as orders.created to billing.
A key matching both an exact and a wildcard binding lists each queue once via the contains check.
A key matching no binding returns an empty Vec<String>.

exerciseSolutions.title: Make the consumer ack only after the durable effect
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Model the two steps as two distinct operations so their ordering is explicit in the code, not implicit in a single fused call. commit writes the durable effect, here a HashMap standing in for the database keyed by message id. ack appends the message id to an ack list, which stands in for telling the broker it may forget the message. handle calls commit first and ack second, and never the other way around. That ordering is the entire point: the durable effect must be safely recorded before the broker is told the work is done.

The duplicate guard sits at the top of handle. Before writing, it checks whether the message id is already in the durable store. If it is, the message has already been processed, so handle skips the write and only re-acks. This is what makes the handler idempotent under at-least-once delivery: applying the same message twice leaves the store in the same state as applying it once, and the second arrival costs only an ack, not a duplicate write. The guard is also what makes redelivery safe rather than dangerous.

The ordering matters because of what the broker does on a crash. Suppose the consumer commits the durable effect and then crashes before it can ack. The broker never received the ack, so it still holds the message as unacknowledged and redelivers it. On redelivery, the duplicate guard finds the id already in the store, skips the write, and acks. The committed-but-not-acked case becomes a harmless redelivery that the idempotency guard absorbs. The forbidden case is the reverse, acking before committing, which the code structurally prevents: no path in handle ever appends to the ack list for a message whose commit did not run.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: commit and ack are separate steps; handle always commits before acking and the duplicate guard re-acks without a second write.
criteria: handle calls commit before ack on every write path, so the durable effect precedes the ack.
An id already in the store re-acks via the guard without a second commit.
Explains a commit-then-crash yields a redelivery the idempotency guard absorbs as a re-ack.
No path appends to acks for a message whose commit did not run.

exerciseSolutions.title: Fix an ack-before-commit consumer
exerciseSolutions.solution:
There are two defects. The first is ordering: the broken consumer acks the broker first and then performs the durable write. An ack is a promise that the work is safely done and that the broker may forget the message. By acking first, the consumer tells the broker to forget the message while the durable effect has not happened yet. If the process crashes in the window between the ack and the write, the broker has already discarded the message and will never redeliver it, so the work is silently lost with no error and no retry. That window is the data-loss bug. The fix is to commit the durable effect first and only then ack, so a crash before the ack leaves the message unacknowledged and the broker redelivers it.

The second defect is unbounded retry of malformed payloads. A malformed or unsupported payload fails the same way on every attempt, so requeuing it forever never makes progress and just blocks the queue behind a message that can never succeed. The fix has two parts. First, classify the failure: a transient failure, such as a temporary database error or a downstream timeout, deserves a bounded retry, while a malformed or unsupported payload is a terminal failure that should go straight to the dead-letter queue without wasting a single retry, because retrying a deterministic failure only delays the inevitable and holds up healthy traffic. Second, make retries counted and capped by an attempt number; once a message exceeds the cap, it too is routed to the DLQ rather than cycling endlessly.

The refactored handle below encodes both fixes. It parses and validates first and sends anything malformed straight to the DLQ. For valid payloads it commits the durable effect and then acks. If the commit fails transiently, it retries while the attempt count is under the cap and dead-letters the message once the cap is reached. The idempotency guard still sits in front, so a redelivery caused by commit-then-crash is absorbed as a re-ack rather than a duplicate write.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Commit precedes ack; malformed payloads dead-letter immediately while transient failures retry under a bounded attempt cap.
criteria: Names ack-before-commit as the cause of silently lost work on a mid-handler crash.
Refactor commits the durable effect before sending the ack.
Retries are counted and capped, and a message over the cap routes to the DLQ.
A malformed or unsupported payload goes straight to the DLQ since it fails identically every time.

exerciseSolutions.title: Design a versioned envelope for mixed deployments
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The envelope wraps the payload with metadata that must travel with every message because the message can outlive the code that produced it. The minimum fields are: schema_version, an integer or semantic version identifying the payload contract; message_id, a stable globally unique identifier (a UUID assigned at publish time, never derived from arrival order); message_type, the routing-relevant name such as orders.created; created_at, a timestamp for measuring message age; and payload, the typed body. Optionally a producer field and a trace/correlation id help observability. The decisive point is that the version belongs in the envelope, not in tribal knowledge, so a consumer reading a message weeks later knows exactly which contract it is looking at without guessing.

A consumer reads schema_version before deserializing the payload. If the version is one it understands, it proceeds. If the version is newer or otherwise unrecognized, it must not crash and must not block the queue by requeuing the message indefinitely behind itself; instead it routes the message to a DLQ (or a dedicated parking queue) so the head of the live queue keeps moving, and the message is held for a newer consumer to drain later once that version is deployed. This keeps a single skewed message from stalling an entire partition during a rolling deploy.

The message_id is the idempotency key, which is what makes replay harmless. The consumer records each processed message_id in its durable store and, on seeing an id it has already committed, acks without reprocessing. Because the id is stable across redelivery and replay, a message replayed weeks later, or redelivered after a commit-then-crash, deduplicates to a no-op rather than producing a second side effect. Finally, to keep a pile-up from staying invisible, expose at least these queue-health signals: queue depth (how many messages are waiting), message age (how long the oldest unconsumed message has sat), retry rate (how often deliveries are being requeued), and dead-letter count (how many messages have been parked as terminal). A growing depth with rising age, a climbing retry rate, or a jumping DLQ count each say the system is backed up rather than merely quiet.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Envelope carries schema_version, stable message_id, and payload; the consumer dedups by id and parks unrecognized versions instead of blocking.
criteria: Envelope carries an explicit schema version, a stable unique message id, and the payload rather than a bare struct.
The message id is the idempotency key, so duplicates and replays deduplicate instead of reprocessing.
An unrecognized version is parked or dead-lettered for a newer consumer rather than crashing or blocking.
Lists queue depth, message age, retry rate, and dead-letter count as the minimum health signals.

exerciseSolutions.title: Bound the local worker budget, not just broker prefetch
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Backpressure has two independent layers, and the exercise forces them apart. The broker layer is prefetch: it caps how many unacknowledged messages the broker will hand a consumer at once. The local layer is the in-process worker queue: it caps how much work those delivered messages are allowed to buffer inside the process before it is drained. Modeling both as separate fields, prefetch and local_capacity, is what makes the difference visible. The trap the chapter warns about is setting prefetch generously and assuming the system is now protected, when in fact a generous prefetch with no local bound simply relocates the pile-up from the broker's queue into the consumer's heap.

The offer method honors the two limits in order. First it checks prefetch: if in_flight has reached the prefetch cap, the broker would not hand over another message, so it returns. Otherwise it tentatively counts the message as in-flight and then checks the local buffer. If the local queue is already at local_capacity, the consumer sheds the work explicitly, incrementing a rejected counter and releasing the in-flight slot, rather than letting the VecDeque grow without bound. Only when both limits allow does the message land in the local buffer. A worker then drains one message per work_once call, completing the work and freeing the in-flight slot so the broker may deliver more.

With prefetch 8, local_capacity 2, and a burst of 5 offered before any worker runs, prefetch alone would have admitted all 5 (it allows up to 8). The local cap is what actually protects the process: the first two messages fill the buffer and the remaining three are rejected, giving buffered = 2 and rejected = 3. Draining the buffer twice yields done = 2. The one-sentence takeaway the exercise asks for: setting prefetch without a local cap does not remove the overload, it only moves it from the broker into the process heap, where it is harder to see and harder to shed safely.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Prefetch and local capacity are modeled as two independent limits; with prefetch 8 but local capacity 2 a burst of 5 buffers 2 and sheds 3.
criteria: Carries a broker prefetch cap and a bounded local worker queue as two independent limits.
A message offered past the local capacity is shed and counted, not appended to an unbounded buffer.
With prefetch 8, local capacity 2, and a burst of 5, the output is buffered = 2, rejected = 3, done = 2.
States that prefetch without a local cap relocates the overload into the process rather than removing it.

labSolution.expectedOutput:
orders.created -> billing,search
orders.cancelled -> billing
unrouted total = 2
labSolution.explanation:
The completed route method is the whole point of the lab: it makes the exchange the single owner of routing policy. It looks up the routing key in the bindings map. On a hit it clones and returns the bound queue names; on a miss it increments self.unrouted and returns an empty Vec. The clone is required because route takes &mut self (it must mutate the counter) yet returns owned Vec<String> to the caller, so it cannot hand out a borrow into the map.

In main, orders.created was bound to both billing and search, so route returns both names and the first line prints orders.created -> billing,search. orders.cancelled was bound only to billing, so the second line prints orders.cancelled -> billing. The two keys orders.refunded and orders.archived have no binding, so each takes the miss branch, incrementing unrouted to a final total of 2.

This is the chapter's direct-exchange model in miniature: the producer side names only routing keys, the exchange owns the binding table, and a key that matches nothing is counted as unrouted rather than silently vanishing, which is exactly what makes a routing gap observable instead of invisible.

reviewAnswers.question: In the publish path, which decisions belong to the producer and which belong to the exchange, and why does that split let teams change routing topology without editing publishers?
reviewAnswers.answer: The producer decides only the routing key, a stable semantic label such as orders.created, and never names a queue. The exchange owns the binding table and the routing policy that maps keys to the set of queues that receive a copy. Because routing topology lives in one place, the exchange, a team can declare a new queue and bind it to an existing key to start receiving copies with no change to any publisher. Putting routing in the producer instead would force every new consumer to trigger an edit and redeploy of every publisher.

reviewAnswers.question: Why must a consumer commit its durable side effect before sending the ack, and what does the broker do with a message that stays unacknowledged?
reviewAnswers.answer: An ack is a promise that the work is safely done and that the broker may forget the message, so committing first guarantees the durable effect exists before the broker is told to discard the message. If the consumer acked first and crashed before committing, the message would be gone with the work never done, a silent loss. While a message stays unacknowledged, the broker holds it and redelivers it (to the same or another consumer), so a commit-then-crash before the ack simply becomes a redelivery the idempotency guard absorbs.

reviewAnswers.question: Since AMQP delivery is at-least-once, what does it mean for a handler to be idempotent, and how does a recorded message id make replay harmless?
reviewAnswers.answer: Idempotent means applying the same message twice leaves the system in the same state as applying it once, so a duplicate delivery causes no extra side effect. Because delivery is at-least-once, duplicates are the design center rather than a rare edge case, and idempotency is the only way to make them safe. Recording each completed message id in a durable store lets the handler detect a redelivered or replayed id and ack it again without redoing the work, so a message replayed weeks later deduplicates to a no-op.

reviewAnswers.question: When should a failed message be retried versus sent to a dead-letter queue, and what goes wrong if a poison message is requeued forever?
reviewAnswers.answer: Retry transient failures, such as a temporary database error or a downstream timeout, under a bounded attempt count, because they may succeed on a later attempt. Send terminal failures, such as a malformed or unsupported payload, straight to the dead-letter queue, because they fail identically every time and a message that exceeds the retry cap goes there too. Requeuing a poison message forever never makes progress and blocks the queue behind a message that can never succeed, which the DLQ exists to prevent by moving it aside so healthy traffic keeps flowing.

reviewAnswers.question: What does backpressure protect against in a broker-based system, and which signals tell you a queue is piling up rather than merely quiet?
reviewAnswers.answer: Backpressure protects against unbounded overload: a queue is a shock absorber, but without a limit it just hides the fact that producers are outpacing consumers until the system falls over. It has a broker layer (capping unacknowledged in-flight messages, for example with a prefetch limit) and a consumer layer (bounded local queues), and it lets the system say no gracefully instead of accumulating work invisibly. The signals that distinguish piling up from merely quiet are queue depth, message age, retry rate, and dead-letter count; a growing depth with rising age, a climbing retry rate, or a jumping DLQ count all indicate a backlog rather than an idle but healthy queue.
